comments.author: Tiberium
comments.textRawHtml:
For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary.

Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation.

The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand:

- The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly

- Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that

- Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage

I just wanted to share this because there's a lot of misconceptions going around about this being a "recomp" or something like that. Decompiling the entire binary (it's about 100MB of real executable machine code) will be a much bigger effort than getting this binary to run.

children.author: Agentlien
children.textRawHtml:
I work with graphics and performance in video games. For the last two years my main focus has been low-level Xbox stuff. It is fascinating both how much stuff is just Windows API and also how many weird platform-specific quirks there are.

Getting the same thing to run on PC and Xbox Series X|S can be such a wild ride. 90% just works, unlike PS5 or Switch where there's a lot of work to get anything running at all. But those last 10% are so full of odd fiddly platform-specific details.

children.author: andai
children.textRawHtml:
I also heard this from devs who release games for windows. The first few weeks after launch are spent full time on fixing weird edge cases (due to the vast diversity of hardware configs), largely graphics related. I heard this even for 2D games with simple graphics!

Seeing this thread initially I was surprised GTA isn't already on PC, but then I remembered it makes sense, ironing all that stuff out can be a big pain.

children.author: elif
children.textRawHtml:
The reason GTA is not already on PC is the same reason GTA is not online yet.

Its not a technical reason or a temporal constraint.

It's because by releasing the same game 3 different times throughout a year, they can maintain lasting cultural relevance.

children.author: rickdeckard
children.textRawHtml:
That's surely a benefit of it, but in terms of pure engineering management it is also more reasonable to not launch for PC at the same time.

Focusing resources to optimize for ~4 targets (2x XBox, 2x PS5) is a better use of time than postponing the ENTIRE launch until all PC-issues are ironed-out.

The least thing you want is a "Cyberpunk 2077" situation where your resources are spread thin and the game only works well on specific configs but is unstable on others, and tanks the experience (and reviews!) for everyone.

In addition, the advanced PC graphics features in your backlog suddenly are no blockers for the launch anymore and you can continue working on them while the console version is shipped.

children.author: alexdoesstuff
children.textRawHtml:
There's fairly limited evidence that there is true double dipping happening, or that there's a profit maximizing motive behind delaying PC version and online. Commercially, it almost surely doesn't make sense to delay PC release or online mode.

For GTA 5, when the PC version was released in 2014, sales increased by about 20M units during the launch quarter, from about 34M units sold before the PC launch to about 54M units sold afterward. The company itself at that point said that it was mostly new players, not people buying twice. And it's still a small share of overall GTA 5 sales which stands at 230M units.

Delaying online is almost surely a commercial negative for the company. They lose out on the revenue from people moving from online to GTA 6 without the possibility of offsetting that loss with similar online-related revenue. For the game to be an economic success, they need to generate more revenue from players than just the initial sale. It's just the economic reality of publishing the game as it is.

children.author: rickdeckard
children.textRawHtml:
> "Delaying online is almost surely a commercial negative for the company."

That's an interesting aspect. The leaks a few months ago showed that Take2 is still making millions per month from GTA V.

Now with the launch of GTA VI you may lose a bit of that revenue because your console players are also busy on GTA VI (having generated a billion USD to offset the loss of revenue though).

But you don't want to replace GTA V online with a less-stable GTA VI and burn that still-stable revenue-stream, so it makes sense to do pure engine bug-fixing with a single-player launch while finishing the online aspects of the game.

It's quite a beauty to observe what a development team can do when given proper time and resources...

children.author: alexdoesstuff
children.textRawHtml:
Their financial reporting suggests they've made ~825M last 12 month on GTA V and Online. That number has been around the same mark for the 3 years prior as well. It's fair to assume that that number with the release of GTA VI is essentially zero now.

They've announced $3.8B in gross sales through preorders and launch day (about 32.5M units). They book around 65% of those gross sales as revenue after sales taxes and platform fees, so they've made ~$2.5B in revenue until launch day and they'll probably end up at at least 2x the figure at year end. But from their perspective, you can only sell the game once and realistically most of their high intention customer-base will have bought the game at the very least by the end of the year.

And from then on, the absence of an online component and the revenue associated with it will start to sting unless they release it quickly.

children.author: rickdeckard
children.textRawHtml:
> "I think it's only a bit disappointing that there isn't a timeline yet for either."

Quite a luxury for a development team. They probably said "let's wait with that commitment until we know what's reported from the field"

PC-support alone must be crazy, e.g. so far their target-platform was only AMD GPU's with AMD x86. Now they need to account for a sea of AMD AND nVidia driver patches, DirectX, different Intel architectures, HDD read-speeds, etc.

It's also worth to note that Rockstar's online architecture is much more dependant on the game itself than other online games, because instead of dedicated Client/Server architecture they use P2P with quite slim backend-servers for orchestration.

One more reason to not rush the Online feature, as they are more vulnerable to cheating than other games...

children.author: etempleton
children.textRawHtml:
I think it is a combination of factors, some of which are legacy. Rockstar has historically always released on console first and then released on PC a full year or more later. This was likely a scope and technical decision more than anything else as consoles were architecturally much different in the PS2 and even PS3 days. Now I think it is a combination of things:

1. Rockstar is obsessed with polish and wants to limit the scope for launch to make sure they deliver the best product they can. Focusing on just the console versions makes sure they don't over reach and design around the PC. The PC version will require additional work as well, so best to just put that to the side and get the console versions out the door.

2. Releasing on PC later allows them to receive additional free PR around the PC release and keep GTA in the media longer.

3. Yes, some people will double dip and buy twice.

The substantiated rumor is that they will release in Q1 which would break from their pattern of waiting a full year or more. I think this is because consoles are much closer to PCs these days and because they are terrified of an early build or a recompiled version showing up on PC before the official release.

I do think they could take the wind out of these projects sails by just announcing a date for PC release, but again, they are going to want to make sure it is ready before giving a date.
